title: Sabbath Gates, Daily Offerings, and Kitchens
summary: The inner east gate opens on Sabbaths and New Moons, when the prince worships at its threshold and the people bow at its entrance. Rules follow for the prince's offerings, for the flow of worshipers through the north and south gates, and for the daily morning offering. The prince may not seize the people's land, and gifts from his estate to servants return at the year of liberty. Ezekiel is shown the kitchens where priests cook the holy offerings and where the people's sacrifices are boiled.
story: The vision continues the regulations that began with the shut gate in chapter 44 and the prince's duties in chapter 45. Here the focus is on the rhythm of worship: weekly Sabbaths, monthly New Moons, yearly festivals, and a daily offering every morning. The prince has a place of honor but not of priesthood, and his worship is joined to the people's. The chapter's middle section returns to the land, guarding the people's inheritance from the ruler's greed, a theme the vision will not let go. Its final scene, the kitchens, brings the grand vision down to the practical matter of cooking sacrificial meals, and prepares for the river that will flow from the temple in chapter 47.
historical:
Sabbath and New Moon were ancient Israelite holy days, often mentioned together (2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 1:13). Under the monarchy the king had a prominent role in temple worship, and some kings abused it; Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense himself (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Ezekiel's prince has a defined place: he enters through the porch of the gate, stands by the gatepost while the priests offer his sacrifices, bows at the threshold, and leaves the same way. He never enters the inner court where the priests serve.

The law of the year of liberty in verse 17 draws on Leviticus 25, where every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, land returned to its original families and Israelite servants went free. There is little evidence that the Jubilee was regularly kept under the monarchy, and Jeremiah 34 records how Jerusalem's leaders freed their slaves during the siege and then took them back. Ezekiel's vision builds the principle into the prince's own estate: his gifts to servants are temporary, so royal land stays in his family, and he has no reason to take land from the people. Verse 18 names the evil directly: evicting people so that they are scattered from their property.
cultural:
Worship at ancient temples was not quiet contemplation in a building. It happened mostly in open courts, with crowds, animals, smoke, and the smell of cooking meat. Many sacrifices, especially the peace or fellowship offerings, were partly burned on the altar and partly eaten by the worshipers and priests in a festive meal before God. That is why the temple needed kitchens. The priests' kitchen is kept apart so that the most holy offerings are not carried into the outer court, where they would transmit holiness to the people (verse 20). The four corner courts, each forty by thirty cubits with hearths along the walls, are where the Levites cook the people's sacrifices.

The rule that worshipers entering by the north gate must leave by the south, and the reverse (verse 9), is partly crowd control on busy feast days. It may also carry a symbolic point: no one leaves God's presence the same way they came in. The daily offering is described as a morning burnt offering only, while the Law of Moses prescribed one in the morning and one in the evening (Numbers 28:3-8). The reason for the difference is not given.
literary: The chapter continues the legal regulations of the vision in three parts: worship on holy days (verses 1 to 15), the prince's inheritance (verses 16 to 18), and a return to the guided tour, as the man leads Ezekiel to the kitchens (verses 19 to 24). The first section is carefully patterned, with repeated phrases about entering and going out, the ephah of grain with each bull and ram, and a hin of oil per ephah. The generosity rule, "as much as he is able" with the lambs (verses 5, 7, and 11), leaves room for freewill giving within the fixed order. The shift from law back to vision in verse 19 reminds the reader that all these regulations belong to what Ezekiel saw, a picture of a restored community rather than a legal code for a courtroom.

outline.t: Sabbaths and New Moons at the inner east gate
The flow of worshipers at the festivals
Grain offerings, freewill offerings, and the daily offering
The prince's inheritance and the people's land
The kitchens of the priests and of the temple

doctrines.note: The gates open and close by God's calendar, and holy food stays in holy places. The chapter shows holiness shaping time, movement, and even cooking, so that all of life around the temple is ordered toward God.
The prince must not evict the people from their inheritance (verse 18). As in chapter 45, the vision builds justice into its structures so that power cannot swallow the vulnerable.

The people bow in worship at the gate on Sabbaths and New Moons, and the prince worships with them, entering when they enter and leaving when they leave (verse 10). Worship is regular, communal, and led by example rather than by privilege.

words.note: Deror, liberty or release. It is the word used in Leviticus 25:10 for the liberty proclaimed in the Jubilee year and in Isaiah 61:1 for liberty to captives. Here it names the year when the prince's gifts return, keeping land within families as God intended.
Shachah, to bow down or worship, literally to prostrate oneself. Both the prince and the people bow at the gate (verses 2, 3, and 9). The ruler and the ruled take the same posture before God.

Tamid, continually or regular. In verse 15 it describes the daily burnt offering, offered every morning without fail. The same word appears in Daniel for the daily sacrifice that the little horn takes away (Daniel 8:11).

Yanah, to oppress or mistreat, used in verse 18 of the prince taking the people's land. The same verb appears in 45:8 and in the Law's command not to mistreat the foreigner (Leviticus 19:33). The vision names oppression by the powerful as a threat to worship itself.

christ: Jesus began his public ministry by reading Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth, announcing that he was sent "to proclaim liberty to the captives" and "to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor" (Luke 4:18-19). The liberty that Ezekiel's vision protects in land law, Jesus proclaims as the release his kingdom brings. The prince who worships alongside the people and does not take their inheritance also points toward the king who shares his inheritance with his people, so that the New Testament calls believers fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The fellowship meals eaten before God in the temple's courts find an echo in the Lord's Supper, where Christ's people eat together in his presence, though the link is thematic. Hebrews teaches that the regular offerings, repeated every morning, looked forward to the one sacrifice that did not need repeating (Hebrews 10:11-12).
questions: The prince worshiped at the gate and the people bowed at the entrance, entering and leaving together. What does it look like for leaders to worship alongside the people they lead?
Worshipers could not leave by the gate they entered. How has meeting God changed the direction of your life?
The vision protects families' land from the powerful. Who in your community is most at risk of losing what they have, and what could protect them?
